newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Hun Sen in control, chaos in parts of Phnom Penh.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen in control, chaos in parts of Phnom Penh.

text.p: Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen took complete control of Phnom Penh and its outskirts on Monday, but his ousted rival Prince Norodom Ranariddh vowed from France to organise resistance.
Troops loyal to First Prime Minister Ranariddh pulled out of their Tang Krasang base near Phnom Penh airport overnight, leaving Hun Sen's forces unopposed.
Ranariddh said his rival had ousted him from power and vowed to organise resistance against Hun Sen.

"Now that he has succeeded in his coup d'etat, he says he has power and legitimacy," Ranariddh said in France in an interview with the newspaper Le Monde. "The resistance will now be organised inside and outside Cambodia."
A wave of looting and violence engulfed parts of Phnom Penh on Monday, and at least one local reporter was shot dead by the bodyguard of a senior official on a city street, police said.
The reporter's identity was not immediately known. There were unconfirmed reports that a second local reporter was also shot in a separate incident.
Muncipal authorities announced later that the 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. curfew imposed over the weekend was being lifted.

The casualty count from the two-days of fighting and Monday's violence was difficult to determine, but one government official said it was as high as 150. He could not say how many were dead or wounded, but hospital sources and police said at least 13 people had been killed.
The rest of the country appeared quiet. But an official loyal to Ranariddh in the northwestern city of Battambang said there had been a brief clash between the two sides there early on Monday.

Hun Sen said in a radio broadcast late on Sunday that Ranariddh, his uneasy coalition government partner since the 1993 elections, was a "traitor and a thief", and that the prince no longer was first prime minister.
Ranariddh left Cambodia on Friday, the eve of the fighting. He said he fled his homeland before the fighting began on the advice of his generals.
In his radio broadcast, Hun Sen also ruled out any intervention by King Norodom Sihanouk, Ranariddh's father, who is in Beijing undergoing medical treatment.
As fighting raged in Phnom Penh over the weekend, the king called for both premiers to visit him in China to try to resolve their differences. But Hun Sen said that would not be necessary.
"It is heard that the king proposes to have reconciliation in Beijing," Hun Sen said. "It is too late and it is not necessary. Everything is over."

The fighting began on Saturday when Hun Sen sent his forces against Ranariddh's men. Hun Sen said the action was necessary because Ranariddh's commandos had been smuggling defectors from the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group into the capital to boost their troop strength.

State television, which has always been controlled by Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP), showed pictures of abandoned, bombed-out buildings where men from Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party had holed up over the weekend.
Many shops and government offices remained closed and shoppers reported exorbitant prices.
Although the fighting was over by Monday, sections of Phnom Penh remained lawless and violent as troops celebrated their victory with an orgy of looting.
"Its out of control. Today was more frightening than the fighting," said one local reporter.
Among the places ransacked and stripped of equipment and valuables was the city's international airport, which has been closed since Saturday because of the fighting.
Keo Sophal, director general of the Civil Aviation Authority, said he hoped the airport would be open by Wednesday.
"Government troops control it again and we will start repairs. We hope to open tomorrow or the day after," he said.
One aviation source in Phnom Penh said the airport runway had been damaged by shellfire and it was doubtful that commercial airlines could land.
In addition to the airport, shops, houses and warehouses in the area also were looted, witnesses said.
Soldiers and civilians were seen driving off in new cars and on motorbikes. Others were carting off televisions and appliances.
Military police and soldiers later tried to restore order, firing shots in the air to disperse crowds, witnesses said.
